This corresponds to the passage in the sutra: "At that time, the impoverished son [developed] the intention for even a single meal."
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the absence of longing.
There are two parts:
At first they accepted [the teachings] without expectation, yet later they remained in their original state;
this refers to the former case.

Subhūti and others, prior to the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, had understood the meaning of emptiness and guarded the Mahāyāna; they were not deluded regarding the Dharma and knew the principles of the Mahāyāna. Nevertheless, they did not give rise to the thought of the Mahāyāna for even a single moment, nor did they have the slightest intention to partake of even one meal of the Mahāyāna Dharma-food that is the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, it was stated previously: "One does not give rise to even a single thought of fond attachment.
The character "悕" (xī) is pronounced with the initial *xū* and the final *jī*; it should also be written as "希" (xī), meaning "to hope for" or "to aspire to."
The Sūtra says: "However, as for where they abide, they have not yet been able to relinquish it.
The commentary states:
This refers to still remaining in their original position.
"Yet that which they abide in" refers to still dwelling within the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), for they have not yet been able to relinquish the inferior mind of those two vehicles.
The Sūtra states: "After a short time had passed, they came to despise their former minds."
The commentary states:
The second major section below illustrates what has now been attained.
It consists of two parts:
"First the father entrusts it, and later the son receives it"—this refers to the section beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One was like a poor son.
Furthermore, the father’s entrustment is twofold:
first, knowing the time has come; second, assembling the multitude for the entrustment.
This is the first [point].

Regarding the phrase "after a short time": because there was slight further progress following the assembly on the *Prajñāpāramitā* and during the assembly on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is called "gradually."
Because they understand the two kinds of emptiness, their intention is vast and far-reaching, and thus they are called "penetrating and serene.
"Penetrating" (*tong*) means opening and reaching through; "serene" (*tai*) means peaceful and stable.
Regarding "accomplishing the great resolve," it is because they previously gave rise to the Great Mind, which was initially generated and subsequently matured over time.
"Contempt for one's former mind" means regretting that one formerly dwelt in the Lesser Vehicle.
"Contempt" (bi) refers to disdain; it means to feel disdain for the mind that previously cultivated the Lesser Vehicle.
Therefore, Śāriputra spoke first, saying: "We have all entered the same dharma-nature.
Why then does the Tathāgata deliver us by means of the Hīnayāna?
This is our own fault, not the World-Honored One's."
"Every time I reproach myself," it is exactly as stated here.
From the scripture's "When the time of death approaches" up to "all have already gathered."
The commentary states:
The second section concerns entrusting the assembly.
It has two parts:
The first is the assembly, and the second is the formal proclamation;
this is the former.
Now, five years had passed since the time of the *Nirvāṇa* assembly when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was held; thus, it is said that the time of his passing was imminent.
In the past, the sons of the great śrāvakas withdrew, while they met with the kinsmen of the bodhisattvas.
The four, beginning with the king, are metaphors for the fourfold assembly; alternatively, as their names suggest, they may be actual representatives of those classes.
Regarding the scripture passage from "He then made a declaration himself" to "to where I am born," the commentary states:
This is the formal announcement below.
There are two parts:
first, restating the past; second, announcing the present—the section beginning with "Suddenly, in this interval" constitutes the latter.
Within the restatement of the past, there are three sections.

First, the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment is cited; second, the subsequent falling back into the cycle of birth and death is cited; and third, the remaining four matters concerning the long duration of expedient means are cited.

This refers to the first: having encountered a Buddha midway, one was unwilling to cultivate the Mahāyāna; thus, one was transformed by means of the Two Vehicles to demonstrate the Mahāyāna, yet showed no aspiration for it. This is the first point.
It is extremely difficult for those of the Two Vehicles to become Buddhas; therefore, I have proclaimed this myself and have not sent others to speak of it.

When I was formerly the sixteen princes, I taught them to resolve upon the Great Mind. Their roots of goodness were born from my own mouth, for they were produced from the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Because that which is born from the Buddha-dharma is truly born.
Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, “In such-and-such a city, for more than fifty years,” the commentary says:
The phrase "receding from" refers to flowing through birth and death.
"A certain city" refers to the Mahāyāna.

Having first encountered [the teaching], one is taught to give rise to the mind directed toward the Mahāyāna; while those of fixed nature in the Mahāyāna or those with superior-grade resolve will certainly not regress or sink, the present discussion concerns those of indeterminate nature and those with inferior-grade resolve.
Having already undergone the cycle of birth and death through successive regressions, he is therefore called the City of Such-and-Such;
he abandoned me and fled.
The character "líng" (伶) is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *-ing* (as in *lángdīng*), and is identical in meaning to "líng" (零).
In the *Qieyun*, "líng" is defined as "a musician," which is not what is clarified here.
The pronunciation of "píng" is *pǐ dīng* (匹丁反); the *Sāncāng* states, "'língpíng' means 'linked and fluttering' (*liánpiān*)."
It also describes the appearance of being solitary. According to the *Qieyun*, "if one's conduct is not upright, one is called *língpíng*.
The character "líng" (竛) has the phonetic *lángdīng* (郎丁反), and "píng" (竮) has the phonetic *pǔdīng* (普丁反); it is also written as *zhēng* (彾) or *yíng* (𢓳).
Furthermore, when walking improperly, one stumbles;
stumbling causes a grunting sound.
Nowadays, the character "páng" (跉跰) is often used instead, though it is not known what this refers to.
Some commentaries explain that "qíngpíng" (跉跰) describes the manner of treading upon dangerous ground.
There is also a version written as "qíngbīng" (跉俜), which signifies a state of being solitary and alone.

Some tread upon the perilous and arduous paths of the five destinies; others wander alone and in hardship, drifting through the five destinies. Because they have abandoned the Buddha and other such parental figures, they are called "solitary."
Although this interpretation may be plausible, I do not know what its basis is.
The pronunciation of "péng" is also *bǔ zhèng* (補諍), which is identical to that of "bèng" (迸).
"Péng" means "irregular," while "bèng" means "to scatter"; neither, however, carries the meaning intended here.

The meaning here is this: having abandoned one's parents and fled, one is constantly unsettled; deprived of companions and left solitary and precarious, one's conduct cannot be upright, and one suffers from fear and hardship.
The Sūtra says: "His original name was so-and-so... [until] he became filled with anxiety and searched for him.
The Commentary states:
This records the remaining four long-term matters within the provisional [teaching].
Having encountered me midway, I am extremely well-acquainted with them, for they have been taught and transformed by me throughout successive lifetimes.
It is because of this familiarity that I recall both their own names and those of others.
Regarding the phrase "formerly dwelling in their original city," it means that when I encountered them midway, I again taught them the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, Śāriputra practiced for sixty kalpas before finally regressing to the Lesser Vehicle; during that intervening time, he encountered the Mahāyāna teachings, which is why I have remained in my original city.
Regarding "seeking with sorrowful concern": because his compassion is profound, it is as if he were filled with sorrow.
Seeing that [beings] are unwilling to practice the Mahāyāna, he employs skillful means to transform them through the two vehicles (*hīnayāna*);
although they attain the fruits thereof, because his compassion is profound, he again reveals the Great Vehicle to them, yet they do not desire it.
These various instances are called "investigation.
Regarding the sutra passage, "Suddenly, in this very place, he reached what this son knows," the commentary says:
This is what is being declared now.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those of indeterminate lineage whose faculties have matured should abandon the *pariccheda* (segmented) body and receive the *parināmika* (transformative) body, turning their minds toward the Mahāyāna."
Therefore, it is said that he was found meeting him at this assembly because their resonance and response were in accord.
Since he had previously been transformed by means of the Mahāyāna, it is said, "He is truly my son," and so forth.
My wealth of bodhi and nirvāṇa is what you, my son, ought to receive; it is yours, being the merit that previously arose from benefiting others and now resides within your own self-benefit.
"This is what this son knows;
I now entrust it all to him.
As the sutra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One arrived spontaneously."
The commentary states:
This son has attained it.

From the outset, he had no intention to seek Buddhahood; yet, when his faculties matured, he spontaneously heard the sutra and was destined to become a Buddha. His name, "No-Mind," signifies that he had no expectations or desires for anything; thus, the true treasury of the Buddha-fruit was naturally obtained.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, "The World-Honored One, the Great Rich Elder... down to 'we have become his sons,'" the commentary states:
This concludes the third section, which summarizes the reception [of the teaching].
There are two parts:

the first correlates with what was previously not hoped for, and the second correlates with what has now been obtained; the section beginning with "Now we finally know that the World-Honored One [possesses] the Buddha’s wisdom" constitutes these.

The initial passage consists of five parts: first, the conjunction with the initial arousal of the mind; second, from "World-Honored One, because of the three sufferings... onwards, the conjunction with the retrogression and wandering in birth and death; third, from "confused and ignorant" onwards, the conjunction with the refusal to cultivate the Great [Vehicle]; fourth, from "Today, World-Honored One, you have caused us to contemplate... onwards, the conjunction with being transformed by means of the Two Vehicles; fifth, from "However, World-Honored One, you previously knew us... onwards, the conjunction with the manifestation of the Great [Vehicle] which was not sought.
It is not appropriate for the Buddha to appear again within the third [interval].
Since one encounters the Buddha in the intermediate period, one is likewise a son of the Buddha; and since one was already a son at the initial encounter, this is omitted from the statement.
The preceding metaphor fully describes how one follows the transformation throughout successive lifetimes, as this has already been established.
This is the first passage. The meaning of "son" (*putra*) is as explained previously.

Since the initial teaching involves generating the resolve for enlightenment while actually remaining in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "resembling a son," in contrast to the true sons of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Alternatively, this general characteristic describes the various followers of the two vehicles as being like the sons of the Bodhisattvas.

Since the Buddha has always taught that those of the two vehicles are also the sons of the Buddha, Śāriputra previously stated: "Now, hearing the Lotus Sūtra, I finally know that I am a true son of the Buddha."
Regarding the sūtra passage from "The World-Honored One arrives" to "experiences various torments," the commentary states:
"Together, these two [factors] cause one to regress and flow through birth and death."

The three types of suffering are: first, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); second, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); and third, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

These refer to the intrinsic characteristic of painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*), as well as those factors—whether faculties (*indriya*) or objects (*viṣaya*)—that are conducive to painful sensation, along with their associated mental states (*samprayuktadharma*).
A portion of the five aggregates constitutes the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); that which is oppressed by adverse conditions is termed "suffering.
Because this very suffering is itself suffering, it is called "suffering-as-suffering.
That is to say, among the eight types of suffering, the first five are all designated as suffering-as-suffering.

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), as well as those factors conducive to pleasant feeling—whether they be faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), or associated mental states (*saṃprayuktadharma*)—are termed the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) because they give rise to distress (*daurmanasya*) at the stage of transformation and decay.
Furthermore, because of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the mind is afflicted and corrupted; this is also called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).

A portion of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is of the nature of the suffering of change; specifically, among the eight types of suffering, the suffering of separation from the beloved (*priyaviprayoga*) and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks (*yadapīcchan paryeṣamāṇo na labhate*) are both the suffering of change.

The specific characteristic of the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), as well as the faculties or objects conducive to that sensation along with their associated mental factors—whether at one time accompanied by the latencies (*dausthulya*) of the two aforementioned types of suffering, never separated from them, and pursued by impermanence and susceptibility to change—is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

It is not only the sensation of equanimity that is termed "suffering of conditioned existence" (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā); rather, the five contaminated aggregates (pañca-skandhāḥ sāsravāḥ) are entirely the suffering of conditioned existence. Thus, within the eight types of suffering, all suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha-duḥkha) is subsumed under this category of the suffering of conditioned existence.
As stated in various passages within the eighth chapter on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are differing explanations:
some state that one undergoes this cycle of birth and death due to falling back from the flow [of the path];
others do not mention such a falling back from the flow of the past, but speak in general terms of being oppressed by the three types of suffering and undergoing various torments.
Regarding the sūtra passage, “deluded and ignorant, they delight in and cling to inferior dharmas,” the commentary states:
these three [types of persons] are unwilling to cultivate the Mahāyāna.
Ignorance (*moha*) is called delusion; hesitation is called doubt.
Because they delight in inferior teachings, they are unwilling to cultivate the Great [Vehicle].
As the Sūtra says: "Today the World-Honored One [offers] the price of a single day's labor."
The commentary states:
The four harmonies transform beings through the two vehicles.
There are two [aspects]:
At first, one acquires [the teaching] based on the Buddha’s words, yet not much; later, when describing one's minor circumstances, one considers it sufficient.
This is the beginning.
"Contemplation" (cintā) refers to the contemplative cultivation of the truths (satya).
"Jian" (蠲) also means to eliminate.

By eliminating the filth of frivolous play and severing the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one applies diligent effort with single-minded concentration over many eons and attains *nirvāṇa*.
"Price of a single day" means that what is obtained is not much.
The essence of the Great Nirvana is attained after three great kalpas and is thus called "priceless";
yet now, liberation is attained in just sixty kalpas—is this not the price of a single day of Nirvana?
Furthermore, the Great Nirvāṇa is called "priceless" because it is perfected in three respects;
yet now one has attained only liberation, not the Great Wisdom Dharmakāya;
within that liberation, one has attained only liberation from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), not liberation from the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

If one attains only the liberation from birth-and-death in segmented form, yet does not attain the liberation from the cognitive obstructions and the transformational birth-and-death, how can this not be considered the price for a single day of nirvana?
Because the essence of nirvāṇa is itself liberation.
The Sūtra says: "Having attained this, one arrives at what has been extensively acquired.
The commentary states:
This passage describes those of inferior disposition who consider their own [attainment] sufficient, due to the mindset of the poor and lowly.
Regarding the section of the Sūtra from "However, World-Honored One" to "the division of the treasure-store," the commentary says:
From here below is the fifth section, showing the great lack of aspiration.
It has three parts:
first, knowing that one’s own inclination is toward the small vehicle, one does not aspire because the Buddha did not say that one would attain [the Great Vehicle].
Second, one has personally attained nirvāṇa; because it is already fulfilled, one does not long for it.
Third, [the teaching] is spoken solely for the sake of bodhisattvas and not specifically for my sake; therefore, one does not long for it.
This is the first [point].
"Attached to inferior desires" means delighting in evil and seeking after the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

The Buddha, knowing that I delighted in the lesser, observed that my faculties were not yet mature and thus set me aside; he did not clearly tell me that I too had the potential for Buddhahood, and therefore I did not aspire to it.
The Buddha has nothing he does not relinquish through discernment; therefore, he discerned and relinquished me.
Regarding the sutra passage, "The World-Honored One has reached the state where there is no volitional seeking," the commentary says:
Having personally attained nirvana, they consider themselves already fulfilled; therefore, they harbor no aspiration for more.

Regarding the phrase "expounding the Tathāgata’s wisdom through the power of skillful means": this first explains the provisional teachings of skillful means, intending to reveal the true wisdom of the Buddha of the single vehicle (ekayāna).

Because I have already obtained the price of nirvāṇa, I consider myself satisfied and regard this as a great attainment; thus, I do not know the reality of the Buddha’s wisdom and therefore have no aspiration for it.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, because we have reached the state of being without aspiration.
The Commentary states:
"This was spoken solely for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, not specifically for my sake; therefore, I do not aspire [to it]."
There are two parts:
first the heading, and second the explanation.
This is the heading.
"This teaching of Prajñā is spoken for us as Bodhisattvas by the power of the Buddha’s wisdom-sustenance; it is not spoken for our sake. Therefore, we have no aspiration for this."

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "It is solely for those who have set out to seek the Mahāyāna that the emptiness of all phenomena is taught. This is precisely the same as the present case.
[The passage from] the Sūtra beginning with "For what reason? up to "truly a son of the Buddha" [corresponds to this].
The commentary states:
This explains the third point, "not desiring.

Knowing that we delight in the Lesser Vehicle, he employs the power of skillful means to clearly and correctly preach the Dharma of the Two Vehicles for us; yet he does not clearly and correctly preach it for those like us, who ought to hear the profound Prajñāpāramitā.

The Buddha merely encompasses the general characteristics and, in accordance with my capacity, has proclaimed the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras; we did not know that our own bodies possessed the portion of the Buddha and the seed of the Buddha, and thus we have truly been his sons, training in the *prajñā*.
It is because of this ignorance that they do not aspire to the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "Now we have finally come to understand up to the teaching of the Mahāyāna Dharma," the commentary says:
The final summary of what has now been attained consists of three parts:

first, the attainment through knowing that the Buddha is not stingy regarding the Mahāyāna; second, the attainment through knowing that the Buddha transforms beings solely by means of the Mahāyāna; and lastly, the concluding summary of what has now been attained.
This is the first passage.
It consists of an initial heading followed by an explanation;
the meaning of the text is thus clear.

The *Upāya-parivarta* states: "If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive them; furthermore, being free from greed and envy, he has severed all evils within the dharmas. Thus it is said.
Now I know that the Buddha is not stingy; it is only that I myself delight in the Lesser Vehicle and am unable to study the Mahāyāna.
If there were one who delighted in the mind of the Mahāyāna, the Buddha would have taught it to them, for he is not stingy.
The character "悋" (lìn) is pronounced with the initial *jin* (進) and the final *fan* (反);
it means stinginess or parsimony. If one cherishes something, that is "惜" (xī); once one has cherished it, one becomes "悋" (lìn). Thus, it is rendered as "鄙悋" (bǐ lìn), meaning base stinginess.
The sutra states: "Now, within this sutra... up to the teaching and transformation through the Mahāyāna."
The commentary states:
This understanding is attained because the Buddha teaches exclusively through the Mahāyāna.
Since this sutra speaks only of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), we know that it takes the One Vehicle alone as its central tenet, rather than taking the single body [of the Buddha] as its central tenet.
In the past, when the Śrāvakas were disparaged, it was solely for the purpose of transforming Bodhisattvas and causing them to study the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Since such was the Buddha’s intention, I have now understood that my previous words—stating that "all these are for the sake of attaining the One Buddha Vehicle and all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)"—were indeed so.

In this current edition, it says "expounding the Mahāyāna," whereas in other editions of this sutra, it also says "expounding the Mahāyāna Dharma"; in this sutra, the force of the meaning is similar in both cases.
The Sūtra says: "Therefore, we have all already attained it.
The Commentary states:
This is the concluding summary of what has now been attained.
Regarding the phrase "the sons of the Buddha have attained": this refers to the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle attained by the Bodhisattvas.

Having now heard this sutra and resolved my mind to seek and proceed toward it, I have already attained all that they have attained; because I have attained them with certainty, it is said that I have "already attained them all."

When Bodhisattvas were first established in the stage of initial resolve in the past, they were just as I am today; since they have already attained the ultimate realization, so too have I. Thus it is said that "all have already attained," for there is no difference in principle.
